tldr: We present a method to identify lower-limb joint encoder zero offsets without external motion-capture systems, using only static double-support stance data with both feet on the ground and a pelvis IMU. Through a Hessian eigenstructure analysis, we uncover the rotational coupling (unobservability) caused by parallel pitch axes in the legs, and demonstrate geometric and algebraic decoupling approaches tailored to kinematic ordering.
hero_caption: The calibration principle of this method. During static double-support contact where both feet are fixed to the ground, the inter-foot relative transform $C_k$ must remain constant whether standing upright or crouching. Combining this with the gravity direction $g$ measured by the pelvis IMU forms an optimization problem solved using only onboard sensors.
overview:
For a humanoid to achieve stable bipedal walking and balance control, an accurate lower-limb kinematic model—especially accurate zero offsets for joint encoders—is essential. Even an error of a fraction of a degree can translate into centimeter-level foot placement errors at the end of the serial kinematic chain. However, setting up external motion capture, laser trackers, or optical markers every time recalibration is needed in the field is very cumbersome. Looking down at one's own feet using head-mounted cameras also suffers from field-of-view limitations in typical standing postures, making foot markers hard to see.

To address this, the authors focused on the robot's own "contact constraints." In a static double-support phase with both feet on the ground, no matter how the robot bends its upper body or knees to change posture, the geometric relative pose (relative transformation matrix) between the feet must remain physically invariant. If joint offsets are miscalibrated, the calculated inter-foot relative pose varies across postures. By optimizing the 12-dimensional offset vector to minimize this dispersion, a self-contained calibration becomes possible using only onboard encoders and a pelvis-mounted IMU.

Furthermore, an intriguing aspect of this work is that it analytically exposes the estimation limits caused by parallel pitch axes (hip, knee, ankle) characteristic of humanoids using Hessian eigenvalue analysis. Because parallel pitch axes have collinear rotational Jacobians, orientation residuals observe only the pitch-offset sum across the joints. The paper analyzes how this coupling can be resolved depending on the hip degree-of-freedom ordering (pitch-first vs. roll/yaw-first) and presents a solution that incorporates a standing-posture knee prior.

In validations using real robots (AGIBOT A2 and A3) as well as simulation, the method consistently recovered artificially injected offsets. On held-out test data, it significantly reduced foot-height residuals, and independent external validation against LiDAR confirmed that leg-odometry vertical drift was suppressed.
contributions: Formulated a self-contained 12-DOF lower-limb offset calibration framework that relies on no external metrology, using only onboard encoders, a pelvis IMU, and static double-support contact constraints.
Formally analyzed the rotational coupling induced by humanoid lower-limb parallel pitch axes using Hessian eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

Clarified the observability differences arising from kinematic ordering (pitch-roll-yaw on A3 vs. roll-yaw-pitch on A2) both theoretically and experimentally, establishing decoupling methods via geometric excitation and a knee prior.

Multifaceted validation on two real robots (AGIBOT A2/A3), generalization evaluation on held-out postures, and external comparison with LiDAR-inertial odometry demonstrating the improvement in contact consistency.

sections.heading: Fixing Joint Offsets Without External Cameras Using Foot Constraints
sections.summary: Humanoid lower-limb joint offsets severely degrade walking stability, but conventional calibration requires external measurement setups. This work introduces an onboard-only framework that leverages the physical invariance of the inter-foot relative transform during static double-support contact alongside a pelvis IMU, addressing the coupling problem from parallel pitch axes.
sections.details:
### The Problem with Joint Offsets and Existing Hurdles
An accurate kinematic model is essential for humanoid robots to establish correct ground contact and walk without losing balance. However, when manufacturing assembly errors and sensor zero misalignments (joint encoder offsets) accumulate along a serial chain, an error of less than 1 degree at each joint can result in centimeter-scale foot placement discrepancies.

The classic way to correct this is using bulky external measurement setups like motion-capture systems or laser trackers. However, this makes routine recalibration in the field difficult. On the other hand, approaches that use onboard cameras to view the feet suffer from the fact that humanoid feet rarely enter the head camera's field of view (FoV) in typical standing postures, leading to poor reliability.

### Leveraging Contact Constraints
This motivated the focus on the physical constraint of "double support (both feet in contact)." As long as both feet are firmly fixed to the ground without slipping, the relative pose of the right foot with respect to the left foot frame (a transformation matrix in SE(3)) must remain constant regardless of the robot's posture. The core principle is to solve for offsets by minimizing the dispersion of this relative pose.

### Challenges of Kinematic Ordering and Pitch Axes
The paper's core contribution lies in clarifying the adverse impact that parallel pitch axes (hip pitch, knee pitch, ankle pitch) have on optimization. Targeting two robots with different kinematic orderings—AGIBOT A2 (roll-yaw-pitch from the base) and AGIBOT A3 (pitch-roll-yaw)—the authors quantify rotational coupling among pitch axes via Hessian eigenvalue analysis, demonstrating how to combine kinematic ordering, posture excitation, and mechanical priors.

captions.F2: Overall calibration pipeline. Static double-support data is collected across multiple postures to construct contact residuals and flat-ground residuals. Alternating between updating the inter-foot relative pose mean and optimizing offsets identifies the 12-DOF parameters.

sections.heading: How Does This Differ from Prior Contact-Based Estimation?
sections.summary: We review closed-loop calibration in manipulators and the use of contact constraints in quadruped and humanoid online state estimation. Relative to prior work (notably Yamane's method), this paper distinguishes itself through an SE(3) dispersion formulation, Hessian eigenstructure analysis of pitch coupling, and the impact of kinematic ordering.
sections.details:
### Robot Kinematic Calibration and the Lineage of Contact Constraints
In robotic manipulation, closed-loop constraints have long been used to identify parameters without external metrology. In legged robotics, foot contact constraints have been widely used in real-time base link state estimation (odometry) via Kalman filtering. However, these methods estimate online dynamic states rather than identifying hardware-inherent, permanent encoder offsets in a batch process.

### Comparison with Yamane's Work and Originality of This Study
A prominent example of humanoid calibration using only encoders, an IMU, and flat-foot constraints is the work by Yamane (2009). Taking this as a starting point, this paper makes three clear distinctions:

- **SE(3) Relative Transform Dispersion Minimization**: While Yamane's method evaluated the height dispersion of individual foot vertices, this method adopts a formulation minimizing the dispersion of the full rigid-body transform (3D position + 3D orientation) between both feet.
- **Analytical Formulation of Pitch Coupling**: It clearly explains the intrinsic loss of observability caused by parallel pitch axes using Hessian eigenvectors.
- **Impact of Kinematic Ordering**: It presents the first systematic analysis of how hip degree-of-freedom ordering affects estimation stability.

captions.F3: The AGIBOT A2 and A3 hardware platforms used in experiments, along with the four primary postures for data collection (normal squat, left lunge, right lunge, wide squat). Acquired entirely with onboard sensors without external equipment.

sections.heading: Alternating Optimization: Minimizing Relative Pose Dispersion
sections.summary: Taking the 12-axis offsets of both legs as variables, a nonlinear least-squares problem is built from inter-foot relative pose dispersion (contact residuals) and pelvis IMU-referenced flat-ground residuals. Alternating between updating the true inter-foot pose mean and optimizing offsets achieves fast and stable convergence.
sections.details:
### Kinematic Model and Offset Representation
The lower-limb model comprises 6 degrees of freedom per leg, totaling 12 DOFs. AGIBOT A3 is arranged from the base as pitch → roll → yaw → knee pitch → ankle pitch → ankle roll, while A2 follows roll → yaw → pitch. The true joint angle is defined as $q_k = q_k^{\mathrm{enc}} + \delta q$, where $q_k^{\mathrm{enc}}$ is the encoder measurement and $\delta q \in \mathbb{R}^{12}$ is a constant offset vector.

### Inter-Foot Consistency Constraint (Contact Residual)
During static double support, the relative pose $C_k$ of the right foot viewed from the left foot frame must remain constant. From $N$ frames in a contact segment, the intrinsic Lie group mean $C^*$ on SE(3) is computed. The deviation of each frame's relative pose from this mean is extracted via the logarithmic map $\mathrm{Log}(C^{*-1} C_k)$ to form the contact residual. Minimizing this ensures that foot placement does not shift across postures.

### Flat-Ground Constraint Using IMU
Inter-foot relative poses alone cannot determine the overall tilt relative to the ground. Therefore, the gravity vector $g_{\mathrm{imu}}$ detected by the pelvis (base link) IMU is utilized. Defining the direction opposite to gravity as vertically upward, flat-ground residuals penalize differences in foot sole heights and deviations of foot normal vectors from the gravity vector (horizontal contact).

### Optimization Objective and Alternating Solver
The objective function is the sum of squared contact residuals, squared flat-ground residuals, and a Tikhonov regularization term (weighted L2 norm) to prevent erratic updates. For A3, an upright knee prior is also added.
Because the mean transform $C^*$ depends on the offset $\delta q$, solving both simultaneously in a single shot is difficult. Hence, an alternating optimization is used: alternating between computing $C^*$ from the current $\delta q$ and updating $\delta q$ with Ceres Solver while holding $C^*$ fixed. This stabilizes and converges within just 3 to 4 outer iterations.

sections.heading: Why Pitch Axes Couple: Geometric Limits Revealed by the Hessian
sections.summary: We prove via Hessian eigenvalue analysis that when knee, ankle, and hip pitch axes are parallel, orientation information observes only the sum of their offsets. Joint ordering determines whether posture excitation can break this degeneracy; if not, an upright knee prior or regularization is required.
sections.details:
### Weaknesses Shown by Hessian Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
Performing an eigendecomposition on the data information matrix $H_{\mathrm{data}} = J_{\mathrm{data}}^\top J_{\mathrm{data}}$ reveals directions with extremely small eigenvalues (near-nullspace). These represent combinations of joint offsets that can barely be estimated from the data.

### Coupling Inherent to Parallel Pitch Axes (Proposition 1)
A humanoid leg has three parallel rotational axes: hip pitch, knee pitch, and ankle pitch. When these axes are coplanar and parallel, the column vectors of the Jacobian for rotational residuals point in the exact same direction (are collinear). Mathematically, the rotational change under differential offset variations is $\delta \phi = a \sum_i \delta q_i$, capturing only the aggregate sum of joint offsets. Differential modes (e.g., hip and ankle moving in counter-phase) are fundamentally unobservable (nullspace) from orientation information alone.
While translation (lever-arm differences) softens this from an exact nullspace into a small eigenvalue (near-nullspace), compact humanoid link lengths and predominantly sagittal motions leave it numerically very weak.

### Decisive Differences from Kinematic Ordering
- **A3 (pitch → roll → yaw)**: Hip pitch is closest to the base. Actuating hip roll and yaw causes the hip pitch axis to misalign from the knee and ankle pitch axes when viewed from the foot. Thus, posture variations (geometric excitation) can break the coupling.
- **A2 (roll → yaw → pitch)**: Because hip pitch, knee pitch, and ankle pitch are arranged consecutively, moving hip roll and yaw keeps these three axes parallel to one another. Geometric excitation cannot break this coupling.

### Recipes for Decoupling: Geometric Excitation and Knee Prior
For A3, adopting postures that excite roll and yaw, combined with a knee prior derived from a brief (~5 s) upright standing pose (mechanical CAD zero $q_{\mathrm{knee}}^{\mathrm{mech}}$), cleanly anchors the remaining knee and ankle pitch degrees of freedom. For A2, fully decoupling is avoided; instead, stronger Tikhonov regularization suppresses parameter drift while tightly bounding the pitch sum.

captions.F4: Information matrix $H_{\mathrm{data}}$ spectra (top) and the pitch components of the three weakest eigenvectors D1–D3 (bottom) across four real-robot postures. A2 (left) exhibits an extremely small minimum eigenvalue, making decoupling difficult, whereas A3 (right) has a relatively compact spectrum and favorable condition number.

sections.heading: Sim and Real Validation: How Well Are Offsets Recovered?
sections.summary: Using simulations and two hardware platforms (A2/A3), the authors conducted artificial offset injection tests, held-out posture foot-height residual evaluations, LiDAR-inertial odometry comparisons, and closed-loop walking simulations. On held-out data, foot-height RMS residuals dropped substantially: 4.26 to 2.20 mm on A3 and 8.03 to 1.43 mm on A2.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Protocol
Experiments on AGIBOT A2 and A3 collected 450 frames for each of four static double-support postures: normal squat, left lunge, right lunge, and wide squat (see Fig. F3). To compare the pure effect of kinematic ordering, equivalent MuJoCo models sharing identical masses and link lengths were also evaluated.

### Artificial Offset Injection Tests (Simulation & Real)
Known offsets were injected in software to test if calibration could accurately recover them.
- **A3 Simulation**: The maximum recovery error was just 0.27 degrees on hip pitch, confirming that errors concentrated mildly in the weakly observed pitch axes as predicted by theory, with high precision across other axes.
- **Real Hardware Repeatability**: Offset increments were consistently recovered across platform-specific configurations. On A2, while individual pitch axes had an RMS error of 0.366 degrees, the pitch sum errors were only -0.0053 and +0.0165 degrees for each leg, verifying that the aggregate sum is robustly observed.

### Foot Flatness Evaluation on Held-Out Data
Calibrating on nominal un-injected hardware and testing on held-out postures yielded notable foot-height residual reductions:
- **A3**: Foot-height RMS residuals decreased from 4.26 mm to 2.20 mm (~48% reduction).
- **A2**: Decreased from 8.03 mm to 1.43 mm (~82% reduction).
This confirms that self-contained optimization substantially improves whole-body contact consistency.

### External LiDAR Validation and Closed-Loop Walking
Comparing leg odometry to LiDAR-inertial odometry (FAST-LIO2) evaluated accuracy against an independent reference. Pitch offsets produce substantial vertical trajectory drift (1.04 m slope per degree), but calibration reduced vertical RMS error by 25.5%, bringing leg odometry close to the LiDAR ground truth. In MuJoCo closed-loop walking simulations (reinforcement learning policy) with 3-degree injected offsets, calibration reduced walking foot-ground RMS deviation from 1190.61 mm to 26.57 mm, preserving stable locomotion.

### Ablation: Posture Count and Prior Effects
Increasing posture count showed that adding diverse postures from 1 to 2 postures dramatically improved the condition number $\kappa(H_{\mathrm{reg}})$ from $1.27 \times 10^5$ to $6.19 \times 10^3$, beyond which gains saturated. In practice, data from just 4 postures is sufficient.

sections.heading: Practicality of Onboard Calibration and Remaining Challenges
sections.summary: The paper demonstrated the effectiveness of lower-limb offset calibration relying solely on encoders, a pelvis IMU, and static double-support constraints. It highlighted weak observability from parallel pitch axes and the importance of kinematic ordering. Absolute identification of individual pitch mechanical zeros and hardware closed-loop walking deployment remain future work.
sections.details:
### Summary
This paper presented a humanoid lower-limb offset calibration method that requires no external metrology, combining double-support contact consistency, pelvis IMU flat-ground constraints, and mechanical priors. Hessian analysis exposed the coupling structure of parallel pitch axes, demonstrating that pitch-first arrangements like A3 have geometric decoupling advantages.

### Limitations and Future Outlook
The method assumes a reasonably flat floor and non-slipping double-support contact. Furthermore, on kinematic orderings like A2, full decomposition of individual pitch axes relies on priors and regularization. Future avenues include investigating techniques to identify absolute mechanical zeros beyond contact consistency and directly integrating the calibration into real-robot closed-loop walking controllers.

takeaways: Without external motion capture, simply shifting postures while keeping both feet on the ground (double support) identifies a significant portion of joint offsets via inter-foot relative pose invariance.
Parallel pitch axes (hip, knee, ankle) common in humanoid legs suffer from an intrinsic near-nullspace, where orientation residuals can only observe their aggregate sum.

Robots with a pitch → roll → yaw hip ordering (e.g., A3) can geometrically break pitch parallelism using roll and yaw excitation, whereas roll → yaw → pitch robots (e.g., A2) maintain parallel axes and must rely on knee priors or regularization.
Large posture datasets are unnecessary; numerical condition numbers saturate quickly with just a few diverse stances (around 4 postures: basic squat, lunges, wide squat).
limitations: Assumes non-slipping static double support on a predominantly planar floor; uneven or slippery terrain may introduce estimation biases.

Decomposing individual offsets within the weakly observed pitch subspace depends on an upright knee prior (from CAD) and Tikhonov regularization, meaning all 12 axes cannot be independently identified from data alone.
Dynamic closed-loop hardware walking tests with calibrated parameters were not conducted; walking evaluations remain limited to simulation and open-loop odometry checks on hardware logs.
